question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [British Presidency Capitals and Headquarters]
wrong_fact: Surat is matched with Fort St. David. Fort St. David was actually located in Cuddalore near Madras, not in Surat.
explanation: The English East India Company established its primary centers around major fortified bases. Fort William was built in Calcutta (Bengal), Fort St. George in Madras (Coromandel Coast), and Bombay Castle was the seat of the Bombay Presidency after it relocated from Surat in 1687. Fort St. David was built near Cuddalore on the Madras coast and served as the temporary headquarters of the Madras Presidency when Fort St. George was captured by the French between 1746 and 1749.

question: Which of the following geographical matches regarding the early territorial and revenue acquisitions of the English East India Company is NOT correct? [EIC Territorial Acquisitions]
options: Northern Circars: Acquired via imperial grant from Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II in 1765
24 Parganas: Zamindari rights granted by Mir Jafar in 1757
Burdwan, Midnapore, and Chittagong: Districts ceded to the British by Mir Qasim in 1760
Salsette and Bassein: Ceded directly to the British by the Treaty of Madras in 1769
wrong_fact: Salsette and Bassein were not ceded by the Treaty of Madras (1769). The Treaty of Madras concluded the First Anglo-Mysore War and established mutual restitution of conquests. Salsette and Bassein were Maratha territories near Bombay and were acquired later (Salsette in 1782 under the Treaty of Salbai).
explanation: The British gradually expanded their territorial and revenue base. Mir Jafar granted the zamindari of the 24 Parganas to the EIC after the Battle of Plassey (1757). Mir Qasim ceded the revenue-rich districts of Burdwan, Midnapore, and Chittagong in 1760. Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, as well as the Northern Circars, to the British in 1765. Salsette and Bassein were Maratha territories, and their acquisition was sought during the First Anglo-Maratha War, with Salsette finally secured under the Treaty of Salbai (1782).

question: Which of the following matches linking the geographical locations of English mints to their historical establishment or monetary impact is NOT correct? [English Mints and Currency Cartography]
options: Bombay Mint: Authorized to coin rupees in the name of the Mughal Empire by the Charter of 1677
Calcutta Mint: Obtained official permission to mint Mughal-style coins (Alinagar/Calcutta rupees) via the Treaty of Alinagar in 1757
Madras Mint: Coined gold pagodas in imitation of local Vijayanagara-style coins since the 1640s
Farrukhabad Mint: Established by the British in the Upper Provinces (modern Uttar Pradesh) to issue standard silver rupees for trade in Rohilkhand and Awadh
wrong_fact: The Charter of 1677 granted by Charles II authorized the EIC to mint coins at Bombay, but they were coined as 'Rupees of Bombaim' and were not initially recognized by the Mughals or allowed to bear the Mughal Emperor's name. Official permission to coin imperial rupees that would circulate throughout the Mughal Empire was only granted via Farrukhsiyar's Farman of 1717.
explanation: The ability to mint currency locally was a key driver of British financial stability and trade supremacy. In Madras, the EIC minted 'Star Pagodas' conforming to regional south Indian standards. Under the Treaty of Alinagar (1757) with Siraj-ud-daulah, the British gained the right to coin sicca rupees in Calcutta. The Farrukhabad mint was later established by the EIC in 1803 to standardize currency in the newly acquired Ceded and Conquered Provinces of northern India. The Bombay mint was active from the 1670s, but its coins were rejected in Mughal territories until Emperor Farrukhsiyar officially legalized Bombay-minted imperial rupees in 1717.
